court: New York Supreme Court, Special Term, Westchester County
holding_summary: The court held that the defendant's operation of a private hotel or boarding house for permanent paying guests, with food and liquor served to guests only incidentally, did not violate a restrictive covenant against business use, following Murray v. Charman. However, when defendant converted a separate annex into a full public restaurant and saloon open indiscriminately to non-guests with no lodging facilities of its own, the court found that distinct use violated the covenant and enjoined it.

quotes.text: the maintenance of a private hotel or boarding house in which the furnishing of food and liquor to its guests, to be served with their meals or in their private rooms, was only incidental to the principal business there carried on, and was not a violation of the covenants in question.
